summary: Redwood AE+SE ran an Optimize walkthrough for NexaPay focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations. Customer is evaluating dedicated vs hosted for payment fraud detection chatflows; main concerns were latency SLOs, cost per 1M requests, and data residency. Agreed to run a short pilot using dedicated pool with KV-cache enabled and run benchmarks against their 3s median latency target.
topics: KV / prefix cache sizing and hit-rate modeling
cost model: tokens/second vs reserved GPU cost
transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-08-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Jared (Head of ML - NexaPay), Priya (Platform Eng), Marco (CTO)
---
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood): Hey everybody, thanks for joining. quick agenda — Ethan and I will run through Optimize recommendations for batching and the prefix / KV cache cost model, and then we can map to your latency / cost targets.
[00:12] Jared (NexaPay): Sounds good — we're mostly interested in lower p99 latency for our fraud chatflow but cost is also a big constraint.
[00:20] Ethan (Redwood): Great. Quick question on traffic: what's your typical request size and session length? you mentioned multi-turn chat earlier.
[00:28] Priya (NexaPay): Average request is about 120 tokens in, responses avg 220 tokens, sessions about 6 turns. Peak traffic is around 400rps, steady around 80rps.
[00:40] Ethan: Perfect, that helps. So for those numbers the first lever we look at is batching — continuous batching in the runtime can boost throughput, but it adds some latency headroom depending on how we configure max wait and batch size.
[00:53] Marco (NexaPay): We're aiming for 300ms median and p99 under 1.2s for the chat endpoint. Is that realistic with batching?
[01:05] Ethan: It's realistic but depends — if you accept small micro-batched queuing (like 5-15ms) you keep median low. The p99 is more sensitive to tail issues and KV cache hit rates.
[01:16] Sofia: I'll pull up the sample cost model — we prepared a spreadsheet that shows reserved GPU hourly cost vs per-token hosted cost; Ethan will show the KV cache hit-rate impacts.
[01:26] Ethan: Slide share: so here is the baseline — dedicated A10-like pool tuning; we assume model is an open 13B quantized variant. For 400rps peak with your token sizes, continuous batching with dynamic max wait of 15ms gives about 2.6x throughput improvement over naive single-call.
[01:44] Jared: When you say dynamic max wait, is that adaptive per route? we have one heavy route and lots of small calls.
[01:52] Ethan: Yes — Redwood lets you configure per-route batching profiles. For heavy routes we set higher max batch and lower max wait; for small calls we bias for low latency.
[02:02] Priya: Does that mean separate endpoints or route rules?
[02:07] Ethan: Route rules — same model version but different batching configs. No need to deploy multiple model instances unless you want variant quantization differences.
[02:15] Marco: Ok. Walk me through KV / prefix cache — we want to avoid regenerating repeated context tokens across a user session.
[02:23] Ethan: Right. Two pieces: prefix (session-level) caching and KV cache which stores transformer key-value states across tokens. For multi-turn chat, KV cache gives the biggest perf win because you avoid re-encoding all prior tokens.
[02:36] Jared: We're currently re-sending full context each turn; migrating to KV cache could drop tokens per request by roughly 60%.
[02:43] Ethan: Exactly — in our model that translates to both latency reduction and token-cost reduction. But it requires sticky routing to the same GPU or a shared cache layer.
[02:53] Priya: Sticky routing concerns me — we run in multiple AZs for HA, how does Redwood handle that?
[02:59] Ethan: Two options: 1) dedicated pool with local KV cache and session affinity within AZ — best latency. 2) private deployment with a shared KV cache store (or we can enable a distributed cache layer) — slightly more complex but maintains HA. We'll send architecture diagrams.
[03:15] Sofia: I'll note that for compliance you asked about KMS and audit logs — we already have integrations and can share SOC2 docs.
[03:24] Marco: Yes please, that helps. Back to the cost model — can you quantify savings?
[03:30] Ethan: Sure — using your numbers, baseline hosted per-token cost at our public API estimate is $X per 1M tokens; with KV cache hit-rate at 70% and 60% token reduction per hit, effective token volume drops ~40-45%, which maps to ~35% cost savings vs baseline hosted. Dedicated with reserved hourly cost shifts to GPU amortization — depending on commit level you could get 30–60% lower unit cost but you take on utilization risk.
[04:00] Jared: That makes sense. Do you have an example calculation in the sheet?
[04:05] Ethan: Yes, in the workbook — I'll share after. Example: 1M requests at 120/220 tokens converts to ~340M tokens; with KV and batching we get to ~200M effective tokens. With reserved capacity the math shows break-even at ~250–300k monthly active users for the model size.
[04:26] Priya: What's the assumption for model latency? are you using a 13B fp16 profile or quantized 4-bit?
[04:33] Ethan: We used a 4-bit quantized 13B variant for the cost model to reflect production-ready quant configs — couple ms slower than fp16 on some workloads but much cheaper. We can also profile your exact model binary.
[04:45] Marco: If we go dedicated, what's the onboarding timeline?
[04:48] Sofia: Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks for integration and benchmarking, then 4-6 weeks for production rollout depending on infra. We'll propose a phased pilot scope.
[04:58] [05:00] Jared: Ok, show us sample numbers for p99.
[05:03] Ethan: (shares chart) Without KV cache p99 is ~1.6s on this workload; with KV cache and session affinity p99 moves to ~0.9s in our simulations — remember we also tune batching thresholds per-route.
[05:17] Jared: That gets us below 1.2s target. Nice. What's the residual cause of tail if we still see spikes?
[05:24] Ethan: Usually network jitter, cold cache misses, or very large single-turn prompts. We recommend a fallback policy: on high latency fall back to a smaller model variant or to hosted region with spare capacity.
[05:35] Priya: How automated is that routing/fallback?
[05:38] Ethan: Built-in. Routed by policy — latency, cost, region. You define SLO thresholds and fallback actions.
[05:44] Marco: Any risk to data residency with that? we need all data to remain in EU.
[05:49] Sofia: You can pin routing by region and restrict fallbacks to compliant regions only. For Private deployments we can keep control plane and models within your VPC.
[05:58] Jared: Quick question — how do you model cache eviction? our sessions are long, some users come back after hours.
[06:05] Ethan: We surface KV cache TTLs and a cost vs hit-rate slider in Redwood Optimize; typical approach: keep hot sessions active with longer TTLs and tier cold sessions to a short-term store. Eviction is LRU plus size-based policies.
[06:20] Priya: Does caching increase memory footprint and GPU utilization?
[06:23] Ethan: Yes more KV cache = more GPU memory reserved per session; it's a tradeoff. Our cost model includes memory footprint assumptions so you can see reserved instance sizes.
[06:33] Marco: For NexaPay, would you recommend prefix cache only or full KV?
[06:38] Ethan: For multi-turn chat where history matters, KV cache is highest value. Prefix cache helps with repeated prompt prefixes across users (e.g., common instructions) — both together are ideal.
[06:48] Jared: Can you walk through a specific example with numbers?
[06:51] Ethan: Sure. Example request: 120 in + 220 out ~340 tokens. Without cache, full decode each turn. With KV cache hit you only send delta tokens (let's say 60 tokens per turn) — so token delta from 340 to 140; that reduces GPU compute time and tokens counted. Multiply across 1M requests and you see cost drop.
[07:17] Sofia: we're seeing some slight transcript stutter from the call, sorry if a prior slide missed — Ethan, next slide is the benchmark plan.
[07:26] Ethan: Benchmark plan: 1) replicate traffic profile with replay, 2) run baseline hosted runs, 3) deploy dedicated pilot with KV cache sticky routing, 4) collect latency, tail, and cost metrics — we'll run 24h and 7-day windows.
[07:39] Priya: For replay can we use sanitized logs? we can't share PII.
[07:43] Ethan: Yes sanitized logs are fine; we only need token-level traces and request timing. We can run in your VPC if you prefer.
[07:50] Marco: Are there any config knobs you recommend out of the gate?
[07:53] Ethan: Start with dynamic batching with max wait 15ms on heavy route, max batch 64; small routes use max wait 3ms. Enable KV cache with 2-hour TTL for active sessions and LRU eviction. For model quantization use q4_k_m with per-layer tuning.
[08:08] Jared: Will those settings be in the pilot config?
[08:11] Ethan: Yes we'll provide a recommended config and we'll iterate after the first 24h run.
[08:16] Sofia: quick pause — Marco, any procurement constraints?
[08:19] Marco: We'll need standard enterprise contract and support; we'd like an SLA for p99 and an option for dedicated reserved billing.
[08:26] Sofia: We can support that; I'll loop in sales ops and legal after the call.
[08:31] Marco: Great.
[08:33] [08:40] Jared: I saw earlier in your notes a mention of model variants — if we fallback to smaller model to handle spikes does that affect output quality?
[08:44] Ethan: It can — that's why Redwood supports A/B rollout and automatic quality checks. You can set hallucination or eval metrics to decide fallback only when quality delta acceptable.
[08:55] Priya: Do you have examples of customers using this pattern in finance?
[08:59] Sofia: Yes, we've got case studies; will send a redacted one from Aurora Finance that shows similar traffic and gains.
[09:07] Jared: Awesome. On the spreadsheet, I noticed a row for "cache hit % sensitivity" — how sensitive is p99 to hit rate?
[09:13] Ethan: Very — below 40% hit-rate the p99 benefit drops off sharply. Hitrate variance is often the biggest uncertainty. Our Optimize tool recommends TTL and batching knobs to push hit-rate higher.
[09:25] Priya: Ok. Anything else on KV cache durability? if GPUs fail are we losing cached state?
[09:30] Ethan: If a GPU node fails, session affinity will failover and you'll get a cold-cache miss. For critical sessions you can replicate KV into a shared store or use Private with distributed cache to reduce cold misses.
[09:44] Marco: Let's talk costs in dollars — can you give a ballpark for monthly reserved cost for a small dedicated pool?
[09:50] Ethan: For a small pool supporting your steady-state 80rps with your token sizes, estimate $6k–10k/month depending on instance type and commit. Peak capacity planning bumps that.
[10:02] Jared: That's in line with our expectation. If we do a pilot, what data will you need from us?
[10:06] Ethan: Sample sanitized logs, target SLOs, security requirements, expected concurrency, and any compliance constraints. We'll produce a benchmark plan and a Shah sheet for cost modeling.
[10:18] Sofia: I'll capture next steps here; we'll send pricing + deck, Ethan will send the workbook, and Jared you'll confirm pilot scope.
[10:26] Jared: Yep will do.
[10:28] [10:30] Priya: Quick question on quotas — if we go hosted initially is there a burst option?
[10:34] Ethan: Yes hosted supports burst through soft limits; Dedicated gives guaranteed throughput.
[10:39] Marco: We're leaning for a dedicated pilot with host fallback — agreeable?
[10:43] Jared: Agreed.
[10:45] Sofia: Great. Any final questions?
[10:48] Marco: No, that covers it for me.
[10:50] Priya: I'm good.
[10:52] Jared: one more — can you include the cost sensitivity analysis for lower hit-rates e.g., 30%/50%/70%?
[10:58] Ethan: Yes that's in the workbook and I'll highlight those rows.
[11:02] Sofia: Ok wrap-up: we'll send materials and propose pilot kickoff week of 2027-08-17. Action items captured. Thanks everyone.
[11:11] End of recording.
